Republicans Are in a Midterm Bind. An Avalanche of Cash Could Move the Needle.
 
Plus, the House has packed and gone away for weeks, and why Trump is going easy on Kevin Warsh—for now
 
 
JULIA DEMAREE NIKHINSON/AP
 

Good morning. 

 

Each day Democrats believe they are expanding the number of House and Senate seats they could snatch away from Republicans in the November elections. The polls right now might favor Democrats, but there is plenty of time between now and Nov. 3.

 

One thing that could change the dynamic is a torrent of ad spending that President Trump-aligned groups are planning to help GOP candidates in the next 6½ weeks.

 

The No Going Back PAC has reserved $82 million, according to AdImpact. 

 

The Safety and Affordability PAC is scheduled to spend $35.7 million. 

 

And MAGA Inc. has reserved another roughly $1 million. 

 

Those totals could easily adjust upward as the PACs plan their buys. Meanwhile, large amounts of money will come in from other GOP corners, according to my colleague Anthony DeBarros.

 

The Senate Leadership Fund has booked $173 million, and the Congressional Leadership Fund has reserved $159 million for ad spending.

 

Democrats will be spending big too, and they could be spreading money out into a larger number of states given how they are trying to create more pathways toward a Senate takeover.

 

The upshot is this: Voter views on candidates can shift a lot between now and November, and ad spending could play a big role in that. At the same time, the 2026 midterm election feels like it started a bit earlier than past races, and voters might have already made up their minds earlier than in the past.

 

There could also be large amounts of money coming in from other groups, like the tech industry (AI, data centers), which feel like they have a lot to gain or lose based on the election’s outcome.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar: The Republican lawmaker from Florida has rolled out an ad criticizing Trump on his immigration enforcement tactics.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president will hold a policy meeting at 11 a.m. ET. He will make an announcement on healthcare at 2:30 p.m. ET.

What I’m Following

 
 
TOM WILLIAMS/CQ ROLL CALL/ZUMA PRESS
 

House lawmakers got an early dismissal. Members are heading home until after November’s elections, reigniting a debate over lawmakers’ work ethic as concerns remain about high gas prices and the dangers of AI. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.) insisted that letting members go this week—rather than later this month—is the best path for GOP candidates in the final campaign stretch.

 

Trump held off on Kevin Warsh—for now. The president wants an interest-rate cut, but on Wednesday his new Federal Reserve chairman oversaw a quarter point rise. Trump gave Warsh a long leash and refrained from name-calling and insults, though the positive relationship might not last if the Fed decides to raise rates again in October.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Red and blue America finally found something to agree on: banning Flock cameras.

 

• U.S. and China agree that AI requires guardrails, but they have very different ideas on how to do it.

 

• The White House withdrew its nominee to lead ICE, after resistance on Capitol Hill and from some administration officials.
